---
title: "Module 3 — Right Ventricular Function"
subtitle: "RV strain, pulmonary embolism, and right heart failure at the bedside"
---

## 1. Clinical question

*What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?*

::: {.callout-note}
**The bedside decision frame:** Two questions in order.

1. **Is the RV dilated or failing?** A visually enlarged RV — approaching or exceeding the size of the LV — is the primary finding. Normal RV is roughly two-thirds the size of the LV on apical four-chamber view.
2. **What is the cause, and does it require immediate intervention?** RV failure from massive PE is a needle/catheter emergency. RV failure from chronic pulmonary hypertension or ARDS needs a different approach. The echo does not always give you the diagnosis — it gives you the hemodynamic phenotype to guide management.
:::

The RV is the chamber most often underappreciated in critical care. It operates as a low-pressure, high-compliance structure that tolerates volume overload relatively well but is exquisitely sensitive to acute pressure increases. When RV afterload rises acutely — as in massive PE — the RV dilates rapidly, shifts the interventricular septum, impairs LV filling, and drives the patient into obstructive shock. Recognizing this pattern quickly and accurately is one of the highest-yield skills in critical care echo.

---

## 2. Image acquisition

*Probe, windows, and technique for this module.*

Use a **phased array (cardiac) probe** on the **cardiac preset**. RV assessment requires at least two views. The apical four-chamber is the primary window; PSAX at the mid-ventricular level provides the D-sign. Subcostal is the fallback in unstable patients.

---

### Apical four-chamber — standard and RV-focused

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/apical+4+normal.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal apical four-chamber — standard, LV-centered"/>

<img src="gifs/RV-focused A4C normal.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal RV-focused apical four-chamber — RV centered in sector"/>
:::

**Two related acquisitions:**

- **Standard A4C** — LV is centered in the sector. Useful for an initial RV:LV size comparison only if the LV is not foreshortened. The RV sits at the edge of the sector and is often clipped, which makes RV size and TAPSE alignment unreliable.
- **RV-focused A4C** — from the standard A4C, slide laterally and rotate slightly so the **RV is centered** in the sector and the full RV free wall from base to apex is in view. ASE guidelines specify the RV-focused view for measuring RV linear dimensions, RV area, and TAPSE. Acquire this view explicitly whenever you intend to quantify RV size or function.

**What you are looking for:** RV size, free-wall motion, septal shape, and longitudinal function. Measure TAPSE on the RV-focused A4C with M-mode aligned with the motion of the lateral tricuspid annulus. A value below 17 mm supports reduced longitudinal function; interpret it with acquisition quality, loading, other RV measures, and the clinical state.

**Avoid the pitfall:** The standard (LV-centered) apical view can foreshorten the LV and artificially make the RV appear larger; conversely, a non-RV-focused acquisition clips the RV and underestimates its size. If RV size or TAPSE matters to the decision, acquire the RV-focused view and confirm in a second window.

---

### Parasternal short axis — mid-ventricular level

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Normal Parasternal Short Axis View.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal PSAX — circular LV for comparison"/>
:::

**What you are looking for:** The LV should appear round (like a donut) in cross-section throughout the cardiac cycle. When RV pressure or volume overload is present, the interventricular septum flattens or bows toward the LV, creating a D-shaped LV.

- Septal flattening in **systole**: RV pressure overload (PE, pulmonary hypertension)
- Septal flattening in **diastole**: RV volume overload
- Septal flattening throughout: both

---

### Parasternal long axis — RV outflow

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Normal Parasternal Long Axis (PLAX) View.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal PLAX — RV free wall and RVOT reference"/>
:::

**What you are looking for:** RV free wall thickness (normal <5 mm; >5 mm suggests chronic pressure overload), RVOT dilation, and subjective assessment of RV size relative to LVOT.

---

### Subcostal

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/normal subcostal view.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal subcostal view — RV free wall reference"/>
:::

**When to use:** First-line in the peri-arrest or ventilated patient. The subcostal view shows the RV nearest the probe and allows rapid assessment of RV size and free wall motion.

---

## 3. Visual global assessment

*Train your eye by comparing normal RV dimensions and function against progressively dilated and depressed RVs. Use the normal clip as your reference.*

---

### Normal RV dimensions and function

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/RV-focused A4C normal.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Normal RV on RV-focused apical four-chamber"/>
:::

RV internal diameter is less than two-thirds the size of the LV. The RV does not extend more than two-thirds to the apex. The interventricular septum is round (not flattened). Free wall motion is brisk and TAPSE is greater than 17 mm.

---

### Dilated and depressed RV

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/RV Failure.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Dilated and depressed RV — RV larger than LV on apical four-chamber"/>

<img src="gifs/A4C - Case 2 Submassive PE — how sick is this RV.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Dilated and depressed RV — submassive PE"/>
:::

RV:LV ratio approaching 1:1 or greater. The RV free wall is hypokinetic. On diastole, the septum may be pushed toward the LV indicating volume overload; on both systole and diastole indicates combined pressure and volume overload. The RA may be enlarged.

- Dilation without hypertrophy may support an acute process, but does not date its onset. Compare prior studies and consider PE, ARDS-related acute cor pulmonale, and RV infarction.
- Hypertrophy supports chronic pressure loading; it does not exclude a new PE or acute decompensation. Measure free-wall thickness at end diastole, preferably subcostally, excluding trabeculations and epicardial tissue.

---

### D-sign (septal flattening)

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/Septal Flattening in Saddle Pulmonary Embolism.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Septal flattening (D-sign) in massive pulmonary embolism"/>

<img src="gifs/PSX - M3 Case 3 ARDS acute cor pulmonale — D-sign.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="D-sign in acute cor pulmonale from ARDS"/>
:::

The interventricular septum flattens or bows toward the LV due to elevated RV pressure or volume. Best assessed on PSAX. Pressure overload causes systolic flattening; volume overload causes diastolic flattening. Septal shift impairs LV filling (ventricular interdependence) and can cause hypotension even with a structurally normal LV. In mechanical ventilation, the D-sign may be accentuated by high PEEP.

---

### McConnell's sign

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/McConnell Sign with RV Enlargement.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="McConnell's sign — RV free wall akinesis with apical sparing"/>

<img src="gifs/A4C - M3 Case 1 Massive PE — McConnell sign and clot in transit.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="McConnell's sign with clot in transit — massive PE"/>
:::

RV mid-free-wall akinesis with relative apical sparing is McConnell's sign. It raises suspicion for PE, but RV ischemia/infarction and other RV disorders can mimic it. Published specificity depends on the comparator population: one PE-versus-RV-infarction study found the sign in 70% and 67%, respectively. The sign alone does not select thrombolysis. Integrate PE probability, ECG, hemodynamics, other RV findings, and alternative explanations. [Casazza et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15664548/).

---

### TAPSE

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/TAPSE cursor alignment A4C.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="TAPSE cursor alignment — M-mode cursor along the lateral tricuspid annulus on RV-focused A4C"/>
:::

TAPSE below 17 mm supports reduced RV longitudinal systolic function when properly acquired. It is angle- and load-dependent and can be affected by cardiac surgery and regional motion. Integrate it with RV size, free-wall motion and other measures; a single value does not establish low output, cause, or urgency. Serial changes may reflect loading or acquisition as well as recovery. [ASE 2025](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PIIS0894731725000379.pdf).

---

## 4. Integration cases

*Cases where the finding changes management.*

---

### Case 1: Massive PE — hemodynamic collapse

**Clinical scenario:** A 55-year-old man on a long-haul flight arrives at a connecting airport and collapses in the terminal. He is brought to the ED with BP 70/40, HR 130, O2 saturation 84% on non-rebreather. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with right heart strain pattern (S1Q3T3).

**What exam would you perform?**
Immediate focused cardiac ultrasound as part of a shock examination. Add lung and proximal venous ultrasound when useful without delaying resuscitation.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/A4C - M3 Case 1 Massive PE — McConnell sign and clot in transit.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Apical four-chamber: severe RV dilation, McConnell's sign, clot in transit — massive PE"/>

<img src="gifs/RV volume overload PSX.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Parasternal short axis: D-sign with RV pressure and volume overload — massive PE"/>
:::

**What you see:**
Massively dilated RV, RV:LV ratio >1. McConnell's sign present. D-sign on PSAX. Plethoric, non-collapsing IVC. No pericardial effusion.

**How does this change management?**
This is a high-probability PE presentation with profound instability and convincing RV pressure overload. If CT cannot be obtained safely and no better explanation is found, activate the PE response team and proceed to urgent reperfusion rather than delaying for CT. Systemic alteplase 100 mg over two hours is an established PE regimen; accelerated peri-arrest dosing must follow the institutional PE/arrest pathway, because an optimal arrest dose is not established. Assess bleeding contraindications. If fibrinolysis is contraindicated, consider mechanical catheter treatment or surgical embolectomy with the specialist team; catheter-directed thrombolysis still exposes the patient to a fibrinolytic. Avoid large empiric fluid boluses and support perfusion while definitive treatment is arranged. [ESC PE pathway](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/41/4/543/5556136), [ERC 2025](https://www.erc.edu/media/wwufbysp/gl2025-06-spec-circ-e.pdf).

---

### Case 2: Submassive PE — how sick is this RV?

**Clinical scenario:** A 42-year-old woman presents with 3 days of pleuritic chest pain and progressive dyspnea. BP 108/72, HR 105, O2 saturation 92% on room air. CT confirms bilateral PE with clot in the main pulmonary arteries. Troponin is positive.

**What exam would you perform?**
Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess RV function and guide risk stratification.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/A4C - Case 2 Submassive PE — how sick is this RV.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="RV dilation on apical four-chamber — submassive PE, Case 2"/>

<img src="gifs/PSX D sign - Case 2 Submassive PE — how sick is this RV.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="D-sign on parasternal short axis — submassive PE, Case 2"/>
:::

**What you see:**
Moderately to severely dilated RV. RV free wall hypokinesis present. No McConnell's sign. TAPSE 12 mm. D-sign on PSAX. LV filling appears reduced.

**How does this change management?**
This normotensive PE has RV dysfunction and myocardial injury and warrants immediate anticoagulation if appropriate, monitored admission, and formal clinical risk assessment. Escalate for deteriorating perfusion or respiratory status. Selected patients with additional distress criteria may be considered for catheter intervention after PE-team assessment of expected benefit and bleeding/procedural risk; RV dysfunction alone is not an automatic indication. The 2026 HI-PEITHO trial used RV/LV ≥1, elevated troponin, and at least two specified BP/HR/respiratory-rate criteria. Measure the RV/LV ratio and assess whether the patient matches a supported treatment pathway. [HI-PEITHO](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41910345/).

---

### Case 3: ARDS and RV failure

**Clinical scenario:** A 67-year-old man with severe ARDS (P:F ratio 90) is on lung-protective ventilation with PEEP 16 and FiO2 0.80. He is increasingly vasopressor-dependent on day 3 of his ICU course. No new fever or culture data.

**What exam would you perform?**
Bedside cardiac ultrasound to assess for ventilator-induced cor pulmonale.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/RV volume overload PSX.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Parasternal short axis: D-sign with RV pressure and volume overload — acute cor pulmonale"/>

<img src="gifs/PSX - M3 Case 3 ARDS acute cor pulmonale — D-sign.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Parasternal short axis: dilated RV with D-sign throughout the cycle — acute cor pulmonale in ARDS"/>

<img src="gifs/M5 Case 2 Plethoric IVC — venous congestion.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Plethoric IVC — non-collapsing, consistent with elevated right-sided pressures"/>
:::

**What you see:**
RV dilated, RV:LV ratio 0.9. D-sign present throughout the cardiac cycle. TAPSE 13 mm. No McConnell's sign. Plethoric IVC.

**How does this change management?**
The supplied findings suggest acute cor pulmonale in severe ARDS; assess other causes of worsening shock as well. Individualize PEEP using recruitability, respiratory mechanics, oxygenation, and hemodynamic response: recruitment and overdistension can have different effects on RV afterload. Limit harmful hypercapnia/acidemia while preserving lung-protective tidal volumes and pressures. With P:F 90, prioritize prolonged prone positioning unless contraindicated. Consider inhaled pulmonary vasodilators as selected rescue therapy, reassessing their effect. Avoid empiric fluid loading in a congested RV and support perfusion. [PEEP/recruitability study](https://academic.oup.com/ajrccm/article/210/7/900/8491230), [ATS ARDS guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10870893/).

---

### Case 4: RV infarct

**Clinical scenario:** A 70-year-old man with an inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) is being transferred for primary PCI. His BP is 82/54 and HR 88. He received sublingual nitroglycerin in the field and his BP dropped to 60 systolic briefly.

**What exam would you perform?**
Rapid focused cardiac echo before transfer.

::: {.callout-tip}
<img src="gifs/A4C McConnell sign RV infarct.gif" style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" alt="Apical four-chamber: McConnell's sign — RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing in RV infarct"/>
:::

**What you see:**
Hypokinetic RV with apical sparing. LV function otherwise preserved.

**How does this change management?**
RV infarct complicating inferior STEMI. RV dysfunction in STEMI carries independent prognostic weight beyond LV function alone — it correlates with higher rates of heart failure, arrhythmias (especially from RCA involvement of the AV nodal artery), cardiogenic shock, and mechanical complications including severe mitral regurgitation.

- **Assess preload and congestion before fluids.** Consider a small challenge only when underfilling may be contributing; stop if perfusion/flow fails to improve or congestion worsens. RV infarction does not require volume loading in every patient.
- **Avoid preload reduction in hypotension or preload dependence.** Concomitant LV failure or congestion changes the assessment; tailor therapy to the whole hemodynamic picture.
- **Inotropic support** may be required if severe RV dysfunction produces low cardiac output.
- **Maintain AV synchrony** — loss of atrial kick is poorly tolerated by the failing RV; arrhythmias are common due to RCA territory involvement.
- **Expedite PCI** — reperfusion of the RCA is the definitive treatment. Early identification of RV dysfunction guides monitoring intensity, mechanical support decisions, and post-discharge care.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Case format reminder:** The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.
:::

## Quiz

::: {.callout-note}
**Q1.** On apical four-chamber, the RV appears as large as the LV. What is your next step before concluding RV dilation is present?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
Confirm in a second window. The apical view can foreshorten the LV and artificially make the RV appear large. PSAX or subcostal view should confirm the finding before acting on it.
:::

**Q2.** The D-sign is present in systole but resolves in diastole on PSAX. What does this pattern indicate?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
Systolic septal flattening indicates RV pressure overload — the RV systolic pressure is elevated above normal (e.g., massive PE, acute pulmonary hypertension). Diastolic flattening indicates volume overload. Flattening throughout the cycle suggests combined pressure and volume overload.
:::

**Q3.** What is McConnell's sign and what condition is it most associated with?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
McConnell's sign is RV mid-free-wall akinesis with relative apical sparing. It is associated with acute PE, but can also occur in RV infarction and other RV disorders. Do not apply a fixed specificity to every population or choose thrombolysis from the sign alone; the module's RV-infarction case illustrates the competing diagnosis.
:::

**Q4.** A patient with massive PE and obstructive shock has a BP of 68/40. Why should you avoid large fluid boluses?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
The RV is already severely distended, so additional volume can worsen RV dilation, septal shift, LV filling, and output. Avoid a routine large bolus. A cautious, measured fluid challenge is reasonable only if underfilling is plausible and a response can be assessed; stop if flow or perfusion fails to improve or congestion worsens. The definitive priority is appropriate reperfusion and support of pressure and oxygenation.
:::

**Q5.** TAPSE is measured at 10 mm in a patient with known chronic pulmonary hypertension. How does this differ from the same TAPSE in a patient who was normal yesterday?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
A newly reduced TAPSE warrants prompt assessment of acquisition, loading conditions, other RV findings, and perfusion. It does not alone prove severe acute RV failure or impending collapse. Chronic PH can be stable or can develop life-threatening acute-on-chronic RV failure. Hypotension, impaired perfusion, and the overall clinical trajectory determine urgency in either patient.
:::
:::

## References and further reading

- [ASE right-heart guideline, 2025](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/PIIS0894731725000379.pdf): acquisition and multiparameter interpretation.
- [ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guideline](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/erj/61/1/2200879): decompensated right heart failure.
- [Casazza et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15664548/): McConnell's sign in PE and RV infarction.
- [International FoCUS recommendations](https://www.pocus.org/wp-content/uploads/pdf/Via-JASE-2014-International-FoCUS-Recommendations-2.pdf): focused cardiac examination versus FAST.
- [Multisociety acute PE guideline, 2026](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.11.005) and [HI-PEITHO trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41910345/): risk-based treatment selection.
- [ERC special-circumstances guideline, 2025](https://www.erc.edu/media/wwufbysp/gl2025-06-spec-circ-e.pdf): PE in cardiac arrest and dosing uncertainty.
- [ATS ARDS guideline, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10870893/) and [PEEP/recruitability study](https://academic.oup.com/ajrccm/article/210/7/900/8491230): lung protection and hemodynamics.
